text: Vital status records whether a patient was alive or deceased at the end of the SEER registry's follow-up period for a given case. It is the prediction target in survival models: a binary outcome reflecting the patient's status at last contact, not necessarily death from the cancer itself.

Survival months is the number of months elapsed from diagnosis to either death or the date of last follow-up recorded in the registry. It is only known retrospectively, after the outcome has occurred, so it cannot be used as an input feature when predicting an undiagnosed patient's future status.

T Stage describes the size and local extent of the primary tumor, from T1 (small, confined) to T4 (large, with direct extension into nearby structures like the chest wall or skin). Higher T stages generally correlate with more advanced local disease.

N Stage describes how far cancer has spread to nearby regional lymph nodes, from N1 (limited nodal involvement) to N3 (extensive involvement). Higher N stage is associated with greater risk of distant spread.

6th Stage is a composite staging category combining T Stage, N Stage, and metastatic status into an overall stage group (such as IIA, IIB, IIIA, IIIB, or IIIC), used clinically to guide treatment intensity and estimate prognosis.

Differentiation describes how closely tumor cells resemble normal breast tissue cells under the microscope. Well-differentiated tumors grow more slowly and resemble normal cells; poorly differentiated or undifferentiated tumors are more abnormal and tend to grow and spread faster.

Tumor grade is a numeric score (commonly 1 to 3 or 4) summarizing how abnormal tumor cells appear and how quickly they are likely to grow and spread, closely related to the differentiation assessment.

A Stage distinguishes between regional disease (cancer confined to the breast and nearby tissue or lymph nodes) and distant disease (cancer that has spread to other organs such as the lungs, liver, or bones), the key distinction for treatment intent.

Tumor size, usually recorded in millimeters, measures the largest dimension of the primary tumor. It is an independent prognostic factor: larger tumors are statistically associated with lower survival, even after accounting for stage and grade.

Estrogen receptor (ER) status indicates whether tumor cells have receptors that respond to estrogen. ER-positive tumors often respond well to hormone therapy and are generally associated with a more favorable prognosis than ER-negative tumors.

Progesterone receptor (PR) status indicates hormone sensitivity similarly to ER status. Tumors positive for both ER and PR typically respond best to hormone therapy and tend to have the most favorable outcomes among receptor subtypes.
Regional Node Examined is the total number of lymph nodes surgically removed and examined during staging. A higher examined count gives a more reliable picture of true nodal involvement.

Regional Node Positive is the number of examined lymph nodes found to actually contain cancer cells. A higher ratio of positive to examined nodes is associated with greater risk of recurrence and lower survival.

Age at diagnosis and race are demographic variables included in SEER data. Studies have documented survival disparities across these groups, though such differences likely reflect a mix of biological, socioeconomic, and healthcare-access factors rather than race itself being a direct biological cause.

Any model trained on SEER data reflects statistical patterns in a historical population and provides a probability estimate, not a certain outcome for an individual patient. It should support, not replace, assessment by a qualified oncologist, and should never be the sole basis for a clinical decision.
